title: A Alibi for the Portrait Revisited
premise: When the coffin of town founder Edmund Vale is exhumed for a land dispute and found empty, estate lawyer Marguerite Okonkwo discovers a second will—one that shouldn't exist—naming a beneficiary who died forty years ago. Her investigation into Vale's disappearance unearths the town's founding sin: a death covered up as an accident, witnessed by a child now old enough to finally speak. As Marguerite closes in on the living person who emptied that coffin, she must decide whether exposing the truth serves justice or destroys the only family the witness has left. The case ends not in a courtroom but in a confession Marguerite chooses to seal inside her own memory—and one forged document she burns.
about_author: Yara Yarrow is a former probate clerk from coastal Maine who spent a decade reading other people's final wishes before writing about them. She writes mysteries about paper trails, small towns, and the lies families tell to survive.

chapters.title: The Second Signature
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. While cataloguing the Vale estate for its centennial settlement, she finds a will dated three days after Edmund Vale's official death, signed in his hand. The emotional beat is quiet dread: Marguerite knows documents lie, but this one lies too well.

chapters.title: Empty Oak
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The exhumation reveals no body, only river stones and a child's tin whistle. The town reacts with grief and fury; the police reopen nothing. Beat: isolation—Marguerite realizes she alone believes the coffin was emptied deliberately, decades ago.

chapters.title: What the Whistle Remembers
chapters.summary: Alternating POV with Ruthie Vale-Coleman, Edmund's elderly daughter. Ruthie recalls the summer of 1984, her father's midnight trips to the quarry, and a boy named Tobias who never came home. Beat: memory surfacing like something drowned.

chapters.title: Three Accidents
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She revisits her three prior 'accident' cases and finds each victim connected to Vale's quarry or his lawyer, Ambrose Pell. Beat: cold clarity—the pattern was always there; she just hadn't been looking at the right name.

chapters.title: The Beneficiary
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The phantom will names Tobias Okoye—her own estranged uncle—as beneficiary. Her family name is stitched into the crime. Beat: betrayal and vertigo as the investigation turns inward.

chapters.title: Ambrose's Ledger
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. Ruthie breaks into the closed law office and finds Pell's ledger: payments to four families, hush money spanning forty years, the last entry made last spring. Beat: complicity revealed—the whole town was bought, gently, one envelope at a time.

chapters.title: Someone Is Reading My Files
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Her office is searched, her copy of the will stolen, and she receives a warning wrapped around a pressed lily—Tobias's flower. Beat: fear sharpening into resolve; time is running out because someone else is closing the case their way.

chapters.title: The Quarry at Low Water
chapters.summary: Dual POV converging. Marguerite and Ruthie find Tobias alive, hidden in plain sight as the cemetery groundskeeper—he faked his death in 1984 after witnessing Pell kill a man, and Edmund helped him vanish, then staged his own exit when dying of cancer. Beat: the truth arrives not as a twist but as grief.

chapters.title: Confession, Unrecorded
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Dying Ambrose Pell confesses everything, begging her to use it legally—but a trial would destroy Tobias and Ruthie both. Beat: the climax is a choice, not a chase; Marguerite weighs justice against mercy with the recorder in her hand.

chapters.title: A Alibi for the Portrait
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, coda. She files a will that gives the town the quarry as protected land, burns Pell's confession, and lets the portrait of Edmund Vale keep its alibi. Final beat: bittersweet peace—some truths are carried, not told, and Marguerite adds this one to the price of her survival.
